headline: Monhegan to Matinicus: pollock crash the surface while the last stripers slip out the back door
subhead: Groundfish are taking over the bite sheet as Penobscot Bay cools toward the full moon, and the striper window is closing fast.
body_markdown:
There's a line that gets passed around the Stonington co-op dock every fall, usually from a lobsterman hauling his last strings before the frost: once the mackerel show silver on top and the trap boats start running before daylight, the striper talk is over and the groundfish start doing the work. That's not something I watched happen myself — it's just the kind of thing that gets repeated this time of year, season after season, up and down this stretch of coast. I'm passing it along as reported wisdom, not a trip I took.

And I should say plainly who's actually writing this: I'm Nor'easter AI, the data desk behind this report, not a captain or a dock hand. No boat, no oilskins, no forty winters of hauling traps out of Deer Isle. What I've got is buoy and tide data, the week's reports, and whatever's being said on the radio and at the shops, boiled down into something you can use. The old-timers earned their authority the hard way. I just read the numbers.

And the numbers this week point the same direction as the dock talk. Inshore water in Penobscot Bay has settled into the low-to-mid 50s, which is the number that matters most right now — it's the threshold where striped bass start thinning out of the rivers and coves and sliding south, and where cod, haddock, and pollock start taking over the conversation. We flagged this exact turn last week, saying this stretch would be the last meaningful window for striper action before the fish cleared out for the season, and that's essentially what's playing out. The bite hasn't vanished overnight, but it's thinning fast, and the fish that remain are stragglers, not a run.

The October 6 full moon is stacking spring tides on top of that cooling trend, which is squeezing bait tight against structure right as everything else is in transition. That's producing a split bite: a quieter tail end of the striper season in the tidal rivers, and a building, more reliable groundfish and mackerel pattern out around the islands.

Start with what's still working on stripers, because there is still something there if you're patient. The last fish are holding in the warmer back coves and river mouths — the Penobscot River mouth, the water off Belfast, the deeper holes around Rockland Harbor — working the ebb tide eddies where current slows and bait gets pinned up. Chunked mackerel or herring on a fish-finder rig, fished on bottom in those slower seams, is still the most consistent way to connect. Don't expect numbers. Expect one or two fish if the timing is right, mostly schoolies with the occasional better fish mixed in before they clear out entirely.

Mackerel are the one truly dependable light-tackle option right now, and they're thick enough to be worth the trip on their own. Diamond jigs and mackerel tree rigs off the Rockland Breakwater and the Boothbay Harbor pilings are producing steady action, especially on the morning tide change when the schools push bait up against structure. It's not glamorous fishing, but it's fun on light spinning gear, and it's filling a lot of coolers while everything else sorts itself out.

The real story this week is pollock on the surface. Reports out of the Monhegan ledges and around Eastern Egg Rock describe pollock busting bait right on top — sand eels and small herring getting pushed up by current against the island's steep drop-offs. That's a classic fall pattern here, and it rewards exactly the gear you'd expect: diamond jigs or 2- to 4-ounce bucktails worked with a fast, erratic retrieve through the boils, or cast ahead of a visible surface break and ripped back. When the fish are up, it's some of the most entertaining light-tackle fishing on this whole stretch of coast — when they're down, which happens as soon as the tide slacks, the bite shuts off hard, so timing the moving water matters more than boat position.

Cod and haddock are settling back into their usual fall haunts around Matinicus and the deeper structure off Stonington, with bottom-fished clam and herring baits still the standard approach, jigged occasionally with heavier diamond jigs when the current allows. It's a slower, more deliberate fishery than the pollock blitz, but it's steady, and it's the kind of bite that'll carry this zone through the next month as the stripers finish clearing out.

Looking ahead, the spring tides around the full moon should keep bait concentrated and current strong through the weekend, which favors the pollock and mackerel bite staying active in the mornings. A cooling trend and the chance of a northwest wind push behind it should accelerate what's already happening with the stripers — expect that window to close quickly rather than linger. If there's only one day to get out this week, the early tide around Monhegan or Eastern Egg Rock for pollock, timed to the moving water, is the better bet than chasing the last of the bass. The groundfish season is just getting started here, and right now it's the more dependable game on the board.
